title: Relational Database – New Notes
subtitle: Tables, keys, SQL, normalization, ACID and OLTP/OLAP — beginner-friendly revision with examples.

what.body: A relational database organizes structured data into tables (rows + columns) and connects those tables using keys and relationships. If the data naturally fits rows and columns with clear links between entities, think relational.
what.example: A Customers table (CustomerID, Name, City) plus an Orders table where Orders.CustomerID points back to Customers.CustomerID. One customer can have many orders, and a JOIN answers questions like: which customer placed order 101?

concepts.body: Table = related data in rows and columns (e.g. Customers). Row/record = one instance (one customer). Column/field = one attribute (Name, City). Schema = the database's structure: tables, columns, types, keys, relationships, constraints.
Uniquely identifies each row. No duplicates, no NULLs. One primary-key definition per table (it may span multiple columns). Example: CustomerID in Customers.
A column that references a key in another table, creating the relationship. Orders.CustomerID references Customers.CustomerID. Memory: primary key identifies, foreign key connects.
Two or more columns that together uniquely identify a row. Neither OrderID nor ProductID alone is unique per order line, but OrderID + ProductID together is.
One-to-one: person → passport. One-to-many: one customer → many orders (most common). Many-to-many: students ↔ courses, normally via a junction/link table (StudentCourses).
INT (IDs, counts), DECIMAL (prices), VARCHAR (names/text), DATE and DATETIME, BOOLEAN/BIT (yes/no). The type decides what a column may store.
Missing, unknown or unavailable value. NULL is not zero, not an empty string, not FALSE.
Rules that protect integrity: PRIMARY KEY (unique row), FOREIGN KEY (valid relationship), NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK (values must satisfy a condition), DEFAULT (value supplied when none is given).
Foreign-key relationships must stay valid: an order must not reference a customer ID that does not exist.
Organizing data into related tables to reduce duplication and improve integrity. Benefits: less redundancy, no inconsistent copies, easier updates.

1NF: one atomic value per cell (split multi-value cells into rows). 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency (non-key columns depend on the whole composite key). 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependency (no non-key column depending on another non-key column). Memory: depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

SELECT retrieves, WHERE filters, INSERT adds, UPDATE changes, DELETE removes, ORDER BY sorts, GROUP BY groups rows (often with COUNT/SUM). Example: SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;
Combine related tables. INNER = matching records only. LEFT = everything from the left table + matching right (gaps become NULL). RIGHT mirrors LEFT. FULL OUTER = everything from both sides.

A transaction is a group of operations treated as one unit (bank transfer: debit A + credit B; COMMIT on success, ROLLBACK on failure). ACID: Atomicity = all or nothing; Consistency = follow the rules (one valid state to another); Isolation = concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other; Durability = committed data survives crashes.

OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) runs day-to-day business: banking, shopping, bookings — frequent inserts/updates on current data. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) analyzes large/historical data for reports and dashboards. Memory: OLTP runs the business, OLAP analyzes it.

examples.title: JOIN customers to their orders
examples.body: INNER JOIN returns only customers that actually have orders, with the matching amount on each row.
examples.code:
SELECT Customers.Name, Orders.Amount
FROM Customers
INNER JOIN Orders
  ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID;

examples.title: Why normalize: the 1NF fix
examples.body: One cell holding two phone numbers breaks 1NF. Splitting into one row per value fixes it.

examples.title: ACID bank transfer
examples.body: Deduct 2000 from Account A and add 2000 to Account B as one transaction. Atomicity: both happen or neither does. Consistency: no negative balances if the rules forbid them. Isolation: a simultaneous transfer can't corrupt the balance. Durability: once committed, the result survives a server crash.

comparisons.title: Normal forms
head: Form
Rule
rows: 1NF + no partial dependency on part of the key
2NF + no transitive dependency via another non-key column

services.name: Azure SQL Database
services.what: Fully managed PaaS relational database on the SQL Server engine.
services.when: You want a managed SQL database without managing infrastructure.
services.scenario: Question says 'managed SQL database' with no VM/server management.

services.name: Azure SQL Managed Instance
services.what: Managed Azure SQL with broader SQL Server compatibility and instance-level capabilities.
services.data: Structured data for migrated SQL Server workloads.
services.when: Migrating SQL Server workloads that need instance-level features, still fully managed.
services.scenario: Question mentions near-full SQL Server compatibility but PaaS management.

services.name: SQL Server on Azure VMs
services.what: SQL Server running on an Azure virtual machine — most control, most responsibility.
services.data: Structured data where OS/VM control matters.
services.when: You need control over the VM and operating system.
services.scenario: Question says 'SQL Server with VM/OS control' or managing the server yourself.

services.name: Azure Database for PostgreSQL / MySQL
services.what: Managed open-source relational database services on Azure.
services.data: Structured data for PostgreSQL or MySQL workloads.
services.when: Your app targets PostgreSQL or MySQL and you want a managed service.
services.scenario: Question names PostgreSQL or MySQL on Azure.

remember: Relational = tables + relationships; row = record, column = attribute, schema = structure.
Primary key identifies a row (unique, never NULL). Foreign key connects tables.
Composite key: multiple columns together form the key. M:N needs a junction table.
NULL is not 0, not empty string, not FALSE.
Referential integrity = foreign keys always point at rows that exist.
1NF = one value per cell. 2NF = no partial dependency. 3NF = no transitive dependency.
INNER = matching only; LEFT = all left + matches; FULL OUTER = everything.
ACID = Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (follow rules), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed survives crashes).
OLTP runs the business (transactions). OLAP analyzes it (reports, trends).
Managed SQL with no servers to manage = Azure SQL Database. VM/OS control = SQL Server on Azure VMs.

quickCheck.q: What uniquely identifies each row in a table?
quickCheck.a: The primary key — unique values, no NULLs.

quickCheck.q: Orders.CustomerID points to Customers.CustomerID. What is Orders.CustomerID?
quickCheck.a: A foreign key — it connects the two tables (one-to-many: one customer, many orders).

quickCheck.q: A cell holds two phone numbers. Which normal form is violated?
quickCheck.a: 1NF — each cell must hold one atomic value; split into separate rows.

quickCheck.q: Debit A and credit B must succeed or fail together. Which property is that?
quickCheck.a: Atomicity (all or nothing) — with COMMIT on success and ROLLBACK on failure.

quickCheck.q: Daily banking transactions vs yearly sales trend analysis?
quickCheck.a: Banking = OLTP (run the business). Sales trends = OLAP (analyze the business).

quickCheck.q: You need SQL Server but must control the OS. Which Azure option?
quickCheck.a: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines. Fully managed with no servers = Azure SQL Database.
